topics.title: How the steering column carries your input
topics.summary: The steering column is the mechanical connection from the steering wheel to the steering gear. Its supported shaft, upper and lower shaft sections, and coupling carry your turning motion toward the road wheels; the nearby control modules have different jobs.

sections.title: Follow the movement from your hands
sections.body: When you turn the steering wheel, you rotate the shaft running through the center of the steering column. Bearings keep that shaft centered. The upper and lower steering-column shafts continue the connection to the steering gear through the coupling. Thinking of it as a chain of connected shafts makes the exploded drawing easier to read: it shows how the pieces join, rather than a set of unrelated parts.

sections.title: What the component map is showing
sections.body: In the [steering-column overview](#/document/G1726383), callout **1** is the column, **2** is the upper shaft, **3** is the lower shaft and **4** is the coupling. The spaces between the pieces in the drawing help you see their connections. The callout numbers identify parts; they are not a removal sequence.

sections.title: Column, controls, lock and assistance
sections.body: The **column** carries mechanical rotation. The **steering column control module (SCCM)** is part of the electrical interface for switches on and around the wheel. The **steering column lock module (SCLM)**, where fitted, locks the column as a theft deterrent. **Electric power-assisted steering (EPAS)** supplies steering assistance with an electric motor. Those names all contain “steering,” but they describe different jobs. Follow the [electrical-component overview](#/document/G1693265) for switches and the [power-steering overview](#/document/G1686673) for assistance.

sections.title: Why the lower shaft gets a separate check
sections.body: The manual identifies the lower steering-column shaft as collapsible and requires it to be measured whenever it has been disconnected from the upper shaft or coupling. That is a specific service requirement, not something to judge from its appearance in the drawing. Keep the [column check](#/document/G1721912) with the relevant removal and installation procedure when working on that connection.

topics.title: Steering-wheel controls and the SCCM connection
topics.summary: The steering column is the mechanical link between the steering wheel and the steering gear. The SCCM is the nearby electronic interface for wheel and column switches; C226A identifies its power, ground, communication and individual control connections.

sections.title: Start with the steering column itself
sections.body:
The **steering column** is the mechanical link between the steering wheel and the steering gear. The wheel turns a shaft supported by bearings inside the column; upper and lower shaft sections and a coupling carry that rotation onward to the gear. The [column overview](#/document/G1726383) shows how those pieces connect.

Several electrical parts live around this mechanical assembly, which makes their names easy to mix up. The **SCCM** handles the electrical interface for switches around the wheel. The separate **SCLM**, where fitted, operates the theft-deterrent column lock. **EPAS** provides steering assistance with an electric motor. C226A belongs to the SCCM’s connections—it identifies neither the mechanical shaft nor the motor that supplies steering assistance.

sections.title: What the SCCM does
sections.body:
The steering column control module—**SCCM** for short—sits with the switches around the column. The left stalk operates the turn signals and beam-selection functions; the right stalk operates the wipers and washer. Buttons on the wheel provide access to functions such as the message center, cruise control, audio and SYNC. Paddle switches provide transmission-shift requests on the applicable automatic-transmission setup. Equipment varies, so use the reference that matches the switches fitted to the car.

The SCCM communicates on **HS2-CAN**, the high-speed Controller Area Network identified in the manual. The assembly also has separate control circuits. That distinction matters: a connector can carry network messages and individual switch signals at the same time. It does not mean every wire has the same electrical behavior.

sections.title: What C226A tells you
sections.body:
**C226A is the 12-cavity SCCM connector identified on harness 14401.** A cavity is a numbered position in the connector shell; a terminal is the metal contact fitted into a used position. The face illustration shows where those positions are, while the table tells you which circuit belongs to each one.

With the drawing oriented as shown, cavities **1–6** run down the left column and **7–12** run down the right. Cavities **6 and 12** are shaded and marked unused in this source view. Match the keyed outline and cavity numbers to the illustration instead of guessing a position from wire color alone. The connector, circuit and terminal identifiers each answer a different question: which plug, which electrical path and which contact.

sections.title: Read the pin list by its job
sections.body:
| Cavity | Circuit | What it belongs to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | RRH02 | Horn-switch circuit |
| 2 | CRW15 | Separate front-wiper high-speed control circuit |
| 3 | VDB25 | HS2-CAN high communication line |
| 4 | VDB26 | HS2-CAN low communication line |
| 5 | GD214 | Ground at the instrument-panel structure |
| 6 | — | Unused in this connector view |
| 7 | SBP13 | Power feed identified with fuse 13 in the source |
| 8 | VDN05 | LIN communication circuit |
| 9 | CET42 | SelectShift downshift-switch circuit, where fitted |
| 10 | CET43 | SelectShift upshift-switch circuit, where fitted |
| 11 | RE406 | Transmission signal return for the shift-switch circuits |
| 12 | — | Unused in this connector view |

**High and low at cavities 3 and 4 name the paired CAN communication lines. They are not fuse ratings or instructions to apply a test voltage.** Likewise, the signal return at cavity 11 has its own circuit identity; do not read it as another label for the structure ground at cavity 5. The original table retains the exact wire colors, gauges, terminal numbers and qualifiers.

sections.title: Follow a wire beyond the connector
sections.body:
A connector view is a close-up; a wiring diagram shows where the circuit goes. In the [wiper wiring diagram](#/document/wiring-081-003), C226A cavity **8** connects through the LIN circuit to the windshield-wiper motor. Cavity **2** follows a separate path to that motor’s high-speed input. The [wiper operation reference](#/document/G1694645) explains that the separate high-speed circuit provides a fail-safe path if LIN communication fails. This is why a wiper function cannot be understood from the word “wiper” beside one pin alone.

The [6R80 paddle-shift diagram](#/document/wiring-030-003) traces cavities **9, 10 and 11** through the clockspring to the downshift and upshift switches. That diagram describes the automatic-transmission paddle arrangement; it does not establish that those switches are present on a manual-transmission car. For a horn concern, follow the [horn operation reference](#/document/G1688197) rather than treating the switch circuit as the horn’s power supply.

sections.title: What to take from this page
sections.body:
Use the cavity number to locate the position, the circuit number to follow the same electrical path in a diagram, and the function and qualifier columns to understand its role and applicability. The “Used” field distinguishes a populated position from one marked unused in this source. The repair-pigtail and terminal part listings identify service wiring parts; they are separate from the SCCM itself.

This table identifies connections. The applicable diagnostic procedure supplies the required test conditions and expected readings. A useful next step is to open the diagram for the feature you are investigating, rather than assuming that a connector label alone tells you how that circuit should be tested.

sections.title: Why replacement includes a scan-tool step
sections.body:
The [SCCM replacement procedure](#/document/G1693270) includes **Programmable Module Installation (PMI)** when a new module is being fitted. In everyday terms, the scan tool handles the configuration work that goes with changing the electronic module. The manual says to begin PMI with the current SCCM still installed and finish it after installation. If the existing module does not respond, the tool may request As-Built Data.

That preparation comes before taking the assembly apart. The procedure then refers to steering-wheel and column-shroud removal and distinguishes the clockspring connector from the SCCM connector. Follow those linked procedures and their safety instructions; this overview is here to explain why the configuration step and the separate connectors matter.

topics.title: The column lock and its separate connection
topics.summary: The steering column lock module is the theft-deterrent device that locks or unlocks the column under the body control module’s command. Its C2434 connector belongs to that lock system, separate from the SCCM switch connections and the electric motor that provides steering assistance.

sections.title: What the lock is there for
sections.body:
Where fitted, the steering column lock prevents the steering wheel from being used to turn the front wheels while the column is locked. The **steering column lock module (SCLM)** operates that mechanism and reports its position or a detected fault to the **body control module (BCM)**. The BCM decides when to command locking or unlocking using information from other systems.

This is different from power steering: the lock secures the column, while EPAS helps you steer. It is also different from the SCCM, which interfaces with the switches around the wheel. Similar names do not make the modules or their connectors interchangeable.

sections.title: Power and messages have different jobs
sections.body:
The [system-operation reference](#/document/G1693266) describes the BCM supplying lock-module power through a relay and exchanging commands over **LIN**, a local communication link. Power lets the device operate; the communication link carries instructions and status. The BCM does not provide power to the lock module while the vehicle is moving or the engine is running.

A lock-system fault can therefore involve the lock module, its supply or its communication—not just a mechanical lock that feels stuck. The source says a detected lock-module or LIN fault can prevent starting. Use its diagnostic path to establish the cause; the symptom alone does not identify a failed part.

sections.title: Read C2434 as the lock connector
sections.body:
**C2434 has four cavities** in this source view. Cavity **1** is marked unused. Cavity **2**, circuit **CDC45**, is the electrical steering-column-lock positive supply. Cavity **3**, **GD214**, is the instrument-panel-structure ground. Cavity **4**, **VDN02**, is the LIN circuit.

The face drawing and original table give the position, wire and terminal details. The [matching security-system diagram](#/document/wiring-112-003) traces those same connections between the lock module, relay, BCM and ground; it is explicitly labeled **Security Pack**, so check the vehicle’s equipment before applying that layout. C2434 is a different shell and circuit arrangement from the 12-cavity SCCM connector [C226A](#/document/connector-C226A).

sections.title: Why a new lock module needs configuration
sections.body:
The [lock-module replacement procedure](#/document/G1702174) requires configuration work when installing a new component. Before removal, the BCM configuration is uploaded to the scan tool; after the new lock is installed, that information is downloaded back into the **same BCM** so it can establish the correct configuration with the new lock module. The procedure also calls for completing PMI, carrying out BCM-to-Electronic-Steering-Column-Lock configuration/training, and checking the BCM for diagnostic trouble codes.

The physical replacement and electronic setup are therefore parts of the same job. The source procedure also includes airbag access and special fasteners, so use the complete sequence and its referenced instructions rather than treating the connector view as a removal guide.

topics.title: Understanding the fuel pump and sender unit
topics.summary: The fuel pump and sender unit combines fuel-delivery hardware with the sensor that measures tank level. This job removes and reinstalls the assembly through its service opening while restoring the tank seal.

sections.title: One assembly carries different functions
sections.body: The pumping hardware supplies fuel toward the engine, while the sender provides level information for the gauge. Electrical and fuel connections therefore serve different purposes within the same assembly. The 5.2L overview identifies two electric pumps; the shared repair name should not be read as evidence that every engine uses identical internals.

sections.title: Why pressure and fuel level both matter
sections.body: The procedure addresses pressure in the supply circuit and liquid level inside the tank separately. Releasing pressure reduces stored force in the lines; lowering the tank level places fuel below the assembly’s mounting flange. Access beneath the rear seat exposes that flange, while the internal tube connection remains another attachment to the assembly.

sections.title: Understanding the installation notes
sections.body: The 2.3L, 3.7L, 5.0L and 5.2L pages share the same overall service sequence. Their new O-ring requirement restores the seal around the opening, and the alignment tabs establish the assembly’s intended orientation. The lock ring secures the flange, making sealing, alignment and retention distinct parts of successful installation.

topics.title: Understanding the right engine mount
topics.summary: The right-hand (RH) engine mount carries engine load while limiting vibration transmitted into the body. Its replacement procedures differ across the 2.3L, 3.7L, 5.0L and 5.2L engines because surrounding equipment and mount arrangements vary.

sections.title: The mount supports and cushions movement
sections.body: The engine produces vibration and reacts against its mounts as it delivers torque. Flexible mount elements allow controlled movement while holding the engine in position. The 2.3L additionally uses fluid-filled, vacuum-switchable mounts whose damping changes under specified operating conditions, making its vacuum connection part of the mount’s function.

sections.title: Access work follows the engine layout
sections.body: The 2.3L automatic branch includes a transmission-tube bracket. The 3.7L procedure moves the air-conditioning compressor aside, while the 5.0L addresses a strut tower brace when equipped. The 5.2L also disconnects oil cooler hoses and concludes with an oil-level check. These differences explain the separate engine procedures.

sections.title: Support details explain the replacement sequence
sections.body: The support arrangement takes the engine’s weight while the mount is released, and both mount connections are addressed to permit the specified movement. The V8 instructions distinguish structural support points from vulnerable fenders. Installation drawings and fastening stages show how the mount and brackets regain their load-bearing relationship.

topics.title: How the fuel supply is organized
topics.summary: The fuel system stores gasoline, delivers it under pressure and meters it into the engine through injectors. These overviews explain the shared components and the important differences among the covered Mustang engines.

sections.title: From storage to metered delivery
sections.body: The saddle-shaped tank stores fuel, electric pumps move it toward the engine, and the fuel rail distributes it to the injectors. Filtration protects small fuel passages from contamination. A check valve retains pressure after pumping stops, while pressure relief protects against excessive pressure if flow becomes restricted.

sections.title: Why the engine version matters
sections.body: The 2.3-liter system uses closed-loop pressure control and a separate high-pressure pump for direct injection. The 3.7-liter and 5.0-liter references describe mechanical returnless systems. The 5.2-liter has two pumps, two control modules and a serviceable inline filter; the other listed engines have filtration serviced with the pump unit.

sections.title: Reading component roles
sections.body: The level sender reports fuel quantity, while pump control governs delivery. Liquid tubes carry gasoline and vapor tubes serve vapor handling. The capless filler is serviced as an assembly. The collision-shutoff description explains how an event signal from the restraints control module enables pumping to be stopped.

topics.title: How the tank and lines supply fuel
topics.summary: The fuel tank and lines store gasoline, deliver it toward the engine and contain its vapor. These overviews describe the shared layout and the fuel-delivery differences among the four engine versions.

sections.title: Storage, delivery and level measurement
sections.body: The saddle-shaped tank accommodates the vehicle’s underbody layout. Electric pumping hardware moves fuel toward the engine, while the level sender reports how much remains. A check valve retains pressure after shutdown, and pressure relief protects against restricted flow. The capless filler provides the refueling entrance, with separate tubing handling fuel vapor.

sections.title: Engine versions use different delivery arrangements
sections.body: The 2.3L overview identifies closed-loop pressure control; the 3.7L and 5.0L identify mechanical returnless systems. The 5.2L uses two electric pumps and two pump control modules. It also has a serviceable inline filter, whereas the other overviews describe an in-tank filter serviced with the pump.

sections.title: Connecting the component descriptions
sections.body: The liquid-fuel, vapor and brake tubes share a protected underbody bundle, but carry separate fluids or vapor in separate circuits. That distinction helps make sense of the line and coupling references. The collision shut-off description concerns an electronic command to stop pumping; it explains why pump operation also depends on vehicle control signals.

topics.title: Understanding Engine Emission Control
topics.summary: Engine emission control includes managing crankcase gases that would otherwise escape into the atmosphere. These references point to the operating descriptions needed to understand the components and their interaction with engine operation.

sections.title: How ventilation reduces emissions
sections.body: Combustion gases that pass the piston rings collect in the crankcase. Routing those gases back toward the intake allows them to enter combustion instead of venting directly outside. Because the gas stream can carry oil mist, crankcase ventilation also needs to manage oil carryover and the amount of gas flowing.

sections.title: Why the operating reference matters
sections.body: The supplied pages refer system operation and component descriptions to the Powertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis (PC/ED) manual. That fuller description supplies the relationships needed to interpret a component’s behavior. The referral alone does not establish a particular valve arrangement, hose route or diagnostic result.

sections.title: Keeping the engine variants distinct
sections.body: The referral applies to the 2.3L, 3.7L, 5.0L and 5.2L engines. Their location references name an oil separator for the 2.3L and a positive crankcase ventilation (PCV) valve for the others. Read the matching operating description to connect the identified hardware with its role in gas flow and oil control.

topics.title: How the 6R80 intermediate clutch works
topics.summary: The intermediate clutch, identified as clutch C, is a hydraulic holding clutch used in second and sixth gears. It restrains a rear sun gear so the planetary assembly can produce those ratios.

sections.title: Holding a gear creates a useful reaction
sections.body: A planetary gearset needs selected members to be driven or held to establish a ratio. The intermediate clutch supplies a holding action by compressing friction plates against stationary support. Shift solenoid C (SSC) controls the clutch C regulator valve, which meters hydraulic pressure to the clutch piston.

sections.title: Why sixth gear has an additional pressure path
sections.body: Although second and sixth use the same clutch, their shift conditions differ. In sixth, pressure routed from the overdrive-clutch latch valve opposes part of the intermediate regulator’s control pressure. This changes the force acting on the regulator and smooths engagement, explaining the extra control passage in the applied-state information.

sections.title: Identify support parts and pressure states
sections.body: The exploded view places the clutch piston, return spring, pressure plate, and retaining ring alongside the center support and case. Plate quantity is model dependent. In the hydraulic views, the clutch C apply circuit is labeled CL C; a separate low-pressure refill supply keeps air out without providing normal clutch clamping force.

topics.title: Understanding intermediate-clutch diagnosis
topics.summary: The 6R80 intermediate clutch, or clutch C, holds a gearset member during second- and sixth-gear operation. Its diagnostic chart investigates missing, unwanted, delayed, slipping, or harsh application of that holding action.

sections.title: Pressure must reach a sealed piston
sections.body: Shift solenoid C (SSC) influences the clutch C regulator valve, which supplies pressure to the clutch piston. The main-control-to-case seal is part of the delivery path. A damaged or obstructed connection can disturb pressure before it reaches otherwise serviceable plates, explaining why this seal appears prominently in the diagnostic reference.

sections.title: Holding too little and holding too long differ
sections.body: Insufficient clamping force allows movement where the gearset needs a stationary reaction. Unwanted application holds a member when another gear requires a different relationship. Sticking valves, passage restrictions, seal problems, and damaged friction parts can affect these behaviors differently, so the chart separates the operating conditions instead of assigning them one common repair.

sections.title: Read from control hardware toward the clutch
sections.body: The source entries span the solenoid, regulator, hydraulic passages, center support, hub, plates, and piston seals. They also include transmission strategy because pressure commands affect engagement quality. Each condition row identifies possibilities for investigation; the associated action supplies the next evidence needed before deciding whether the fault lies in control, fluid delivery, or mechanical parts.

topics.title: Mustang Body Materials
topics.summary: The body-construction reference identifies the materials used in individual Mustang panels and reinforcements. It helps connect a damaged component to the repair rules appropriate for its metal and structural role.

sections.title: Why neighboring panels use different steels
sections.body: An outer panel provides shape, while hidden reinforcements can carry substantial structural loads. The reference identifies mild steel in many panels, boron steel in selected reinforcements and martensitic steel in the rocker reinforcement. Different material properties let each part serve its intended role within the assembled body.

sections.title: Material identification comes before repair choice
sections.body: Steel strength depends on its composition and processing, and heat or deformation can alter its behavior. The construction maps therefore lead into the metal-repair specifications. A nearby mild-steel panel's repair method does not establish what is permitted for a high-strength reinforcement behind it.

sections.title: Reading colors and body-style views
sections.body: The legend assigns colors to material families, such as yellow for mild steel, red for ultra-high-strength martensitic or boron steel, and purple for aluminum. Item tables identify the actual component. Coupe and convertible views differ, and the battery tray is specifically identified on the right side only.

topics.title: Front subframe service on the 2.3L
topics.summary: The 2.3L EcoBoost front subframe is a bolted structural assembly carrying suspension, steering and engine-mount functions. Removing it separates several load-bearing and control connections, so the procedure coordinates their support and reconnection.

sections.title: A shared foundation for connected systems
sections.body: Suspension arms locate the wheels from the subframe, while the steering gear acts through the tie rods. Engine mounts transfer engine load into the same structure. The 2.3L’s switchable mounts also use vacuum connections, which explains the mount hoses and reservoir connections appearing in this procedure.

sections.title: Why support and separation are carefully ordered
sections.body: Once the engine mounts are disconnected from the subframe, another support must carry the engine in its normal position. Steering shafts, electrical wiring and clipped brake lines also cross the removal boundary. The procedure manages those connections so lowering the structure does not pull on attached components.

sections.title: Reference marks preserve the starting geometry
sections.body: The subframe marks record its position relative to the body before removal. Restoring that relationship limits unintended movement of suspension mounting points, while the final front-toe check evaluates wheel direction. Replacement-fastener instructions and steering-column seal notes address joint integrity and protection of the passenger-compartment opening.

topics.title: Where rear suspension diagnosis begins
topics.summary: The rear suspension supports the vehicle and guides the rear wheels as they move over the road. This reference directs diagnosis to the general suspension procedure because rear-end concerns can involve tires, loading, alignment and several mechanical components.

sections.title: Rear-wheel behavior comes from a complete assembly
sections.body: The upper and lower arms guide the wheel knuckle, springs carry load, and shock absorbers control movement. Toe links influence wheel direction, while the stabilizer bar resists body roll. A change in any of these relationships can alter the way the rear of the car feels.

sections.title: Why this page redirects to broader diagnosis
sections.body: A sensation felt at the rear does not necessarily identify a rear suspension part. Tire condition, unequal loading and alignment can create overlapping symptoms. The general diagnostic procedure establishes those basic conditions and then separates concerns such as lean, excessive movement and abnormal tire wear.

sections.title: Treat the reference as a starting point
sections.body: This page supplies a referral rather than a standalone test sequence or replacement decision. The rear component overview helps identify the parts involved, while the general symptom chart provides the diagnostic branches. Keeping those roles separate avoids reading a short cross-reference as evidence that a particular component has failed.

topics.title: The rear coil spring
topics.summary: The rear coil spring supports vehicle load and compresses as the rear wheel moves upward. Its seated position and spring force help establish ride height while allowing the suspension to absorb road irregularities.

sections.title: The spring stores energy as it compresses
sections.body: A coil spring resists compression by storing elastic energy, then releases that energy as it extends. The rear shock absorber controls the resulting motion so it settles. The spring’s upper and lower seats direct its force into the intended body and lower-arm contact areas.

sections.title: Why the job includes the lower arm
sections.body: The spring sits in the rear lower arm, so the referenced arm procedure manages the supporting structure and spring compression needed for access. The spring page also calls attention to the upper seat because a damaged or incorrectly positioned seat can alter how the spring bears against its support.

sections.title: Read the short page with its supporting procedure
sections.body: The spring reference identifies the component change and its upper-seat requirement, while the lower-arm reference contains the related support and reassembly details. Those instructions belong together because the spring stores force within the assembly. Correct seating is part of restoring the load path, not simply making the spring fit.

topics.title: Convertible passenger upper side-airbag connection
topics.summary: On convertible Mustangs, the passenger upper side airbag provides supplemental head protection during certain side impacts. Connector C3465 carries the paired electrical deployment connections for this seat-mounted restraint.

sections.title: An electrical command activates the restraint
sections.body: An airbag inflator responds to a controlled electrical deployment command by generating the gas that fills the cushion. The paired wires form part of that deployment circuit. Their positive and negative labels describe the dedicated connection to the restraint controller, rather than a general accessory supply and body ground.

sections.title: Distinguishing the head and torso restraints
sections.body: The upper side airbag mounts on the outboard side of the front passenger seat and protects the occupant’s head. It is distinct from the side airbag that protects the torso. The coupe uses a side curtain for head protection instead. The connector chart’s generic seat-mounted side-airbag wording makes the component name and circuit identity especially important when matching this connection.

sections.title: Using the view as an identification reference
sections.body: The connector face, circuit identifiers, and wire colors associate each cavity with its deployment path. The pigtail listings identify service connection options, not a diagnostic method. This page contains no restraint depowering or testing sequence, so any circuit diagnosis depends on the applicable supplemental restraint system (SRS) procedure.

topics.title: Convertible driver upper side-airbag connection
topics.summary: On convertible Mustangs, the driver upper side airbag provides supplemental head protection during certain side impacts. Connector C3464 connects this seat-mounted restraint to its dedicated electrical deployment circuit.

sections.title: Head protection at the seat
sections.body: The upper side airbag attaches to the outboard side of the driver’s front seat. It protects the head, while a separate side airbag protects the torso. The coupe uses a side curtain for head protection instead. These are different restraint assemblies, even though abbreviated connector descriptions can use similar side-airbag wording.

sections.title: A paired deployment connection
sections.body: An electrical deployment command activates the inflator, generating the gas that fills the cushion. The two listed connections form the driver upper side-airbag deployment circuit. Their positive and negative labels identify the dedicated restraint-controller paths; they do not describe an ordinary accessory supply and chassis ground.

sections.title: Match the component as well as the connector
sections.body: C3464 identifies the driver upper side-airbag connection, while the face view and circuit table identify its individual cavities. The harness and service-part entries help identify the connection hardware. Similar connector shells do not make different restraint devices interchangeable. This view provides identification information; depowering, connector handling and electrical diagnosis follow the applicable supplemental restraint system (SRS) procedure.

topics.title: The downstream heated oxygen-sensor connection
topics.summary: The heated oxygen sensor labeled HO2S #12 monitors exhaust after the catalyst in the listed first-bank or single-bank position. Connector C1570 carries both its heater circuit and its exhaust-sensing signal paths.

sections.title: Sensing and heating perform different jobs
sections.body: The sensing element responds to oxygen remaining in the exhaust, providing information used to assess catalyst operation. Its electric heater brings the element toward its useful operating temperature. Heater current supplies thermal energy, while the sensor signal carries measurement information, so the two functions share a connector without being the same circuit.

sections.title: The controller needs a dependable signal reference
sections.body: The table lists protected heater power, a Powertrain Control Module (PCM) heater-control path, a sensor signal and return-related entries. A heater concern can delay useful sensing, while a signal-path concern can distort or interrupt the reported measurement. Identifying the affected path matters before drawing conclusions about the sensor or catalyst.

sections.title: Match the return entry to the wiring variant
sections.body: Alternative return-circuit descriptions and supply-wire sizes appear in this connector reference. They need to be matched to the applicable wiring configuration rather than assumed to operate simultaneously. The post-catalyst description identifies the sensor's functional position, while the male-face orientation and harness identifiers establish how to interpret the connection drawing.

topics.title: Passenger-window control on memory-equipped vehicles
topics.summary: The passenger-window regulator motor raises and lowers the door glass. This sheet shows how power, door-module commands and shared window inputs reach it on vehicles with memory equipment.

sections.title: Motor power and direction commands are separate
sections.body: The motor assembly has battery supply, ground and delayed-accessory connections, together with up and down inputs from the Passenger Door Module (PDM). Power provides the energy to move the glass; direction inputs request the movement. Keeping those roles distinct makes the circuit easier to understand than treating every wire as a motor feed.

sections.title: The window also receives shared information
sections.body: A global input connects the motor to Body Control Module B, and an ajar input provides door-state information. These paths explain why the local window is part of wider vehicle operation. The Body Control Module (BCM) also contains the delayed-accessory relay shown here, linking window electrical availability to accessory-power control.

sections.title: Keep the equipment qualification in view
sections.body: MEMORY is the sheet’s equipment qualification. The convertible note applies specifically to the continuation through C314 toward the rear-window sheet, rather than restricting the entire passenger-door circuit to convertibles. The accessory-delay relay is identified as non-serviceable, so its symbol does not imply a removable plug-in part. Supply labels, ground references and continuation markers connect this sheet to the supporting diagrams.

topics.title: Understanding a Battery Drain Check
topics.summary: A battery drain check measures electrical current leaving the battery while the parked vehicle should be resting. Its purpose is to separate expected standby use from a load that continues consuming excessive energy.

sections.title: An ignition-off vehicle still uses some power
sections.body: Electronic modules can remain active briefly after shutdown and then enter lower-power states. Some functions continue drawing standby current even afterward. A module that stays awake, or a lamp that remains on, removes stored battery energy over time, so a discharged battery does not by itself prove the battery is defective.

sections.title: Why the resting state must be preserved
sections.body: The reference requires a charged battery and time for the vehicle to settle before evaluating current. Opening circuits or triggering vehicle activity can restart module wake-up behavior and change the reading. Equipment-dependent activity, including software updates where supported, must be understood rather than mistaken for an unexplained parked-vehicle load.

sections.title: Reading current changes as circuit clues
sections.body: Current measures the rate of electrical charge flow from the battery; battery voltage alone does not identify the drain. A decrease when a circuit is isolated identifies a contributing branch, not automatically a failed module. The reference specifically recognizes that an external input can keep a healthy module awake, and restoration requirements vary with fitted equipment.

topics.title: Left Rear Noise-Control Microphone
topics.summary: Connector C4828 serves the left rear active noise-control microphone. The microphone converts cabin sound into an electrical signal so the noise-control system can observe the sound it is intended to reduce.

sections.title: Sound becomes a feedback signal
sections.body: A microphone responds to changing air pressure and produces a corresponding electrical waveform. In active noise control, that measurement helps the system account for unwanted sound within the cabin. Carefully timed sound from the audio system can then reduce selected noise through the interaction of sound waves.

sections.title: Why the microphone uses a paired connection
sections.body: The connector lists positive and negative ambient-noise microphone paths. These carry the microphone’s electrical information as a pair, rather than identifying a conventional power feed and body ground. An interruption or unwanted electrical disturbance can change the information reaching the noise-control system without changing the actual noise source.

sections.title: Matching the correct microphone
sections.body: The left-rear component name distinguishes this microphone from other microphones in the vehicle. The circuit wording identifies its ambient-noise role, while an additional housing position is unassigned. This reference establishes the connection and signal pair; it does not supply microphone sensitivity values or prove that a cabin-noise concern originates in the microphone.

topics.title: Convertible rear-window and mirror heating circuits
topics.summary: The rear-window heater and heated mirrors use electrical resistance to warm their surfaces and improve visibility. This convertible wiring sheet shows the defrost relay, control connection, protected supplies and ground paths, with additional equipment qualifications on the mirror branches.

sections.title: Electrical resistance produces useful heat
sections.body: Current flowing through the rear-window element produces heat in the glass, helping clear condensation and frost. Mirror heating works on the same basic principle. Because heating requires appreciable electrical energy, the drawing includes protected supply paths and a relay rather than depicting the dashboard control as carrying every heater's operating current.

sections.title: The relay separates request from load
sections.body: The Front Controls Interface Module (FCIM) connects to the rear-window defrost relay circuit in the Battery Junction Box (BJB). The sheet also shows the mirror branches and their grounds. Displaying these paths together helps explain how a control request, a supply problem and a local heater connection represent different possible circuit concerns.

sections.title: Read the variant and supply labels carefully
sections.body: The CONVERTIBLE heading applies to this sheet. Within it, the dashed mirror-branch outlines identify the without-memory arrangement and the right-hand-drive alternative. Those local labels must stay with their respective branches. Hot at all times and hot in start or run describe different supply conditions. Connector and ground references connect the schematic to identification pages; the repeated mirror symbols show labeled alternatives rather than extra mirrors.

topics.title: Door and B-pillar side-impact sensor circuits
topics.summary: Side-impact sensors provide crash information to the restraints control module (RCM). This sheet identifies separate driver-door and passenger-door sensor circuits, plus left-hand and right-hand B-pillar sensor circuits within a coupe-only branch.

sections.title: Sensors inform the restraint decision
sections.body: The supplemental restraint system (SRS) uses sensor information to assess a crash and determine whether appropriate restraints should deploy. A side-impact sensor supplies an input to that decision; it is not itself an airbag. Separate sensor identities allow the controller to distinguish information arriving from different parts of the vehicle.

sections.title: Dedicated feed and return pairs matter
sections.body: The sheet labels a feed and return for each sensor connection at the RCM. Door-sensor circuits also pass through identified inline connections. Those distinctions help locate the electrical path named in a diagnostic reference without confusing the driver-side, passenger-side, door or pillar sensor with another component.

sections.title: Use the schematic within the restraint procedure
sections.body: The dashed coupe outline surrounds only the B-pillar sensor circuits; the door-sensor circuits appear outside that outline. Keep this qualification with those B-pillar branches rather than applying it to the entire sheet. Connector references support identification, not an invitation to test them independently. The page requires consultation of the workshop manual because improper restraint-circuit troubleshooting can cause unintended deployment and injury.

topics.title: Mirror turn-signal circuit connections
topics.summary: The exterior-mirror turn lamps repeat the vehicle’s direction indication where other road users can see it. This without-memory wiring sheet connects their branches to body-control outputs and grounds, with China-specific continuations to the rear-lamp circuits.

sections.title: Electronic outputs control the indication
sections.body: The Body Control Module (BCM) has outputs labeled for the left and right rear turn lamps, with field-effect transistor (FET) switching identified on the drawing. The sheet traces related turn-signal branches to the exterior mirrors. These electronic outputs switch lamp circuits in response to the vehicle's signaling commands.

sections.title: The mirror branch belongs to a larger circuit
sections.body: The continuation references connect this page to the wider turn-signal, stoplamp and hazard-lamp diagram. Splices show where conductors join, and the mirror grounds complete their electrical paths. This context helps distinguish a concern limited to a mirror branch from one involving a connection shared with other lamps.

sections.title: Observe the market and equipment labels
sections.body: WITHOUT MEMORY is the heading for the whole sheet. The smaller dashed China outlines qualify the branches continuing to sheet 90-6; they do not make the entire mirror circuit China-only. Hot at all times describes supply availability, not continuous illumination. Left-hand and right-hand mirror identifiers separate the sides, while connector and ground references lead to their supporting views.

topics.title: Passenger Seatback Climate Harness Junction
topics.summary: C316 joins the passenger seatback climate-control harnesses. It carries the electrical paths for the blower, temperature sensing and the device that heats or cools the air delivered through the seatback.

sections.title: The seatback conditions air, then moves it
sections.body: The climate-controlled seat uses a blower assembly containing a fan and a Thermo-Electric Device (TED). The TED heats or cools incoming cabin air, and the blower sends that conditioned air through passages in the seat foam. The connector table calls the TED connections heater circuits, but this assembly supports both heating and cooling. Its separate blower-speed and temperature-sensor paths carry control and feedback information.

sections.title: Several circuit types cross one junction
sections.body: The connector brings these related functions together without acting as a control module itself. An interruption here can affect a power path, a control path or temperature feedback depending on the circuit involved. That is why identifying the actual circuit matters more than treating every connection as a heater feed.

sections.title: Compare the two harness faces
sections.body: The male and female tables show the mating sides of harnesses 14D233 and 14D230, with many housing positions unused. Circuit identifiers connect the climate-control device, blower and temperature-sensor paths across the junction. The two faces use different wire-detail entries in places, so keep each face associated with its listed harness. This connector reference does not establish its precise physical position within the seat.

topics.title: Coupe B-Pillar Side Impact Sensor
topics.summary: The coupe’s B-pillar side impact sensors supply crash information to the Supplemental Restraint System (SRS). Secure mounting couples each sensor to the vehicle structure, while its electrical connection carries information to the restraints controller.

sections.title: How crash information is used
sections.body: The Restraints Control Module (RCM) evaluates inputs from multiple sensors to decide whether a crash requires restraint deployment. The side impact sensor contributes information about vehicle motion. Deployment depends on the combined inputs and crash severity, so this sensor is one part of a wider decision-making system.

sections.title: Why attachment matters
sections.body: The repair calls for smooth mating surfaces that allow the sensor to sit flush against its mounting surface. That attachment couples the sensor to the vehicle structure whose motion it measures. The connector and mounting bolt therefore serve different purposes: one carries information, while the other establishes the physical mounting.

sections.title: Understanding the service sequence
sections.body: The procedure brackets sensor removal with the specified SRS depowering and repowering procedures because the restraint controller has stored backup energy. The repair text lists both coupe and convertible trim-removal references, but the wiring diagram identifies the B-pillar sensor pair within its coupe-only branch. Those cross-references do not establish that the pair is fitted to the convertible. Match the actual sensor and body style before choosing the access reference, and retain all restraint-system handling and mounting instructions.

topics.title: Left Seatback Climate Blower Connection
topics.summary: C3034 connects the left front seatback blower assembly on vehicles with climate-controlled seats. This assembly does more than move air: its thermoelectric device heats or cools cabin air before the blower delivers it through the backrest.

sections.title: Heating and cooling happen in the assembly
sections.body: The blower assembly contains a fan, a Thermo-Electric Device (TED) and a temperature sensor. The TED changes the air temperature, while the fan moves the conditioned air through passages in the seat foam. This explains why a connector titled blower motor also includes circuits labeled heater: the assembly combines airflow and temperature control.

sections.title: Different circuits serve different jobs
sections.body: The primary assignments identify driver backrest heater and fan pairs. The front-seat operating description explains that the seat climate controller regulates the TED and blower, using temperature feedback. Electrical power for conditioning air and the information used to control it serve distinct purposes, even though their connections meet at the same assembly.

sections.title: Keep the conflicting catalog labels visible
sections.body: Some remaining entries use passenger-indicator and driver-heater-switch wording even though this is the left backrest blower connection. Those labels do not establish extra indicator lamps inside the blower. Keep the original circuit identities and use the applicable schematic to resolve their precise functions; do not silently substitute a pin assignment from another seat connector.

topics.title: Right Seatback Climate Blower Connection
topics.summary: C3039 connects the right front seatback blower assembly. On climate-controlled seats, this assembly conditions cabin air and distributes it through the backrest so the occupant can receive heating or cooling.

sections.title: A blower and a temperature-changing device work together
sections.body: The assembly contains a fan and a Thermo-Electric Device (TED), with a temperature sensor providing feedback. The TED heats or cools the incoming air. The blower then sends it through the foam passages toward the seat surface. Airflow and temperature change are separate functions within one service assembly.

sections.title: Why the connector has more than motor wires
sections.body: The assignments include passenger backrest heater connections, fan connections, a blower-speed control and temperature-sensor paths. The heater wording refers to the conditioning side of the climate-seat assembly; it should not imply that the complete assembly only heats. The speed-control path carries a command, while the temperature paths report the condition being controlled.

sections.title: Identify the backrest separately from the cushion
sections.body: The backrest and seat cushion have separate blower assemblies. This page identifies the right backrest connection in harness 14D233, so a similar-looking cushion connector is not interchangeable identification evidence. Keep the sensor-return and fan-return labels distinct, and use the original face view when matching the listed circuits.

topics.title: Left Seat Cushion Climate Blower Connection
topics.summary: C3035 connects the left front seat cushion blower assembly. Its thermoelectric device changes the temperature of incoming cabin air, and its fan distributes that heated or cooled air through the cushion.

sections.title: Conditioned air reaches the seating surface
sections.body: The climate-controlled cushion uses an integrated blower assembly containing a fan, a Thermo-Electric Device (TED) and a temperature sensor. The seat controller manages temperature and airflow together. The cushion therefore has both a thermal function and an air-moving function, rather than relying only on a heating wire beneath the upholstery.

sections.title: Power, speed control and feedback are distinct
sections.body: The table identifies driver cushion heater connections, fan connections, a blower-speed control and cushion-temperature paths. The heater label is the circuit catalog wording for the assembly that supports heating and cooling. The temperature signal tells the controller about the assembly’s condition; it does not supply the energy used to move air.

sections.title: Repeated rows do not add another heater
sections.body: Some heater circuit entries repeat with different wire-size details. Preserve those alternatives instead of reading them as additional independent heating devices. Match the left cushion component and harness 14D231 to the face view, then use the applicable wiring configuration for the listed wire details. The right cushion and both backrests have their own connections.

topics.title: Right Seat Cushion Climate Blower Connection
topics.summary: C3040 connects the right front seat cushion blower assembly. The assembly heats or cools cabin air and moves it through the cushion, giving the seat’s temperature controls a physical effect at the seating surface.

sections.title: Heating, cooling and airflow share an assembly
sections.body: A Thermo-Electric Device (TED) changes the temperature of air entering the blower assembly. The fan carries that air through passages in the cushion foam, while a temperature sensor reports the assembly’s condition to the seat climate controller. The seat system operates independently of the cabin climate-control system.

sections.title: Read the heater label in its system context
sections.body: The connector lists passenger cushion heater and fan pairs, a blower-speed control and temperature-sensor paths. The heater wording does not limit the assembly to heating: the system description includes both heating and cooling operation. Power paths, the blower command and temperature feedback have separate roles even though they occupy one connector.

sections.title: Keep cushion and backrest identities separate
sections.body: This connection belongs to the right cushion in harness 14D230. The right backrest uses a separate blower assembly and connector. The unused entry and the sensor-return label should be retained as shown; the latter is a measurement path, not a reason to substitute an arbitrary body ground.

topics.title: Seat Climate Module Power and Thermal Outputs
topics.summary: C3265A connects the power and temperature-conditioning circuits of the front Seat Climate Control Module (SCME). The module controls heated or cooled airflow for the front seat cushions and backrests on vehicles equipped with climate-controlled seats.

sections.title: The controller manages air temperature
sections.body: Each cushion and backrest blower assembly includes a Thermo-Electric Device (TED), a fan and a temperature sensor. The SCME coordinates their operation to produce the selected heating or cooling effect. The device changes air temperature, and the blower delivers that air through the seat foam; this is more than an ordinary seat-heater circuit.

sections.title: This connector groups the thermal power paths
sections.body: The lettered assignments identify separate driver and passenger cushion and backrest heater pairs, along with run/start power and ground. Heater is the catalog label for the conditioning-device paths in this heated/cooled seat system. Keeping the seat and cushion/backrest designations intact matters because each path serves a particular part of the system.

sections.title: One module has several electrical interfaces
sections.body: C3265A is a connector on the controller, not a blower or an inline harness junction. Other SCME connectors carry temperature feedback, blower control and network communication. The ground and supply entries here support module operation; they should not be confused with each individually controlled output pair.

topics.title: Seat Climate Module Temperature Feedback
topics.summary: C3265B is a signal connector on the front Seat Climate Control Module (SCME). Its assignments include seat-temperature feedback, which helps the controller manage the assemblies delivering heated or cooled air through the front seats.

sections.title: Feedback tells the controller what is happening
sections.body: The cushion and backrest blower assemblies contain temperature sensors along with fans and Thermo-Electric Devices (TEDs). The SCME uses feedback while controlling heating, cooling and airflow. A requested temperature setting and an actual temperature reading are different pieces of information: the controller needs both a desired result and information about the system’s response.

sections.title: These are measurement paths, not heater feeds
sections.body: The clearly named entries include passenger cushion temperature, passenger backrest temperature and driver cushion temperature, each with an associated return. Those circuits report conditions rather than providing the power that changes air temperature. Treat each sensor and return as its own measurement relationship when reading the table.

sections.title: Do not guess functions from an inconsistent label
sections.body: The remaining populated descriptions include passenger-indicator and driver-heater-switch wording. This page alone does not establish how those entries relate to the missing driver-backrest temperature labels. Preserve the listed circuit identities and resolve them with the applicable schematic. C3265B is only one connector on the SCME, so it does not show all module supplies or outputs.

topics.title: Seat Climate Module Blower and Network Connections
topics.summary: C3265C connects the front Seat Climate Control Module (SCME) to blower-related circuits and the vehicle’s medium-speed communication network. These paths let the controller receive seat-climate requests and manage airflow through the front seats.

sections.title: Airflow carries the heating or cooling effect
sections.body: The seat’s Thermo-Electric Devices (TEDs) condition cabin air, while the blower fans move that air through the cushion and backrest foam. Blower control is therefore a separate job from changing air temperature. The SCME manages both functions, using commands from the seat controls and feedback from the blower assemblies.

sections.title: Network messages and fan circuits do different work
sections.body: The table lists a Medium-Speed Controller Area Network (MS-CAN) high/low pair, passenger cushion and backrest blower-speed controls, a driver cushion speed control, and fan pairs. The network pair carries messages; the fan paths provide electrical operation, and speed-control paths carry commands. Sharing the connector does not make those functions interchangeable.

sections.title: Retain the unresolved catalog description
sections.body: One populated entry is labeled passenger indicator low rather than a blower-control function. Keep that wording and its circuit identifier visible until the matching schematic resolves it. Unused positions do not imply missing wires, and this connector does not include every thermal-output or temperature-feedback path on the SCME.

topics.title: Driver Seatback Climate and Lumbar Harness Junction
topics.summary: C3050 joins harnesses 14D232 and 14D231. Its assignments combine driver seatback climate-control circuits with lumbar-adjustment circuits, bringing different seat functions through one separable harness connection.

sections.title: The climate assembly changes and moves air
sections.body: The climate-controlled backrest uses a blower assembly containing a Thermo-Electric Device (TED), fan and temperature sensor. It delivers heated or cooled air through the backrest foam. The driver backrest heater and fan pairs listed here belong to that system; the heater wording should not reduce its purpose to heating alone.

sections.title: Lumbar adjustment has a different mechanical job
sections.body: The table also names a driver lumbar pump circuit and an upper-cell deflate-solenoid circuit. Those functions concern the seat’s support adjustment, rather than conditioning airflow. The inline connector carries their existing circuits across the harness boundary; it does not decide how much lumbar support or seat heating the occupant receives.

sections.title: Follow each face’s actual assignments
sections.body: The male and female faces share the principal function labels, with alternative wire-size entries in places. Other populated descriptions use passenger-indicator and driver-heater-switch wording. Keep those original labels rather than inferring extra lamps or substituting another connector’s pinout. Circuit identity, harness identity and the applicable schematic establish which path is being followed.

topics.title: Driver Seat Climate Harness Junction
topics.summary: C315 joins harnesses 14D231 and 14A005 across driver-seat climate-control circuits. It carries paths associated with cushion and backrest temperature conditioning, fan operation and temperature feedback.

sections.title: The seat delivers heated or cooled air
sections.body: Climate-controlled seat blower assemblies combine a Thermo-Electric Device (TED), fan and temperature sensor. The TED conditions cabin air, and the fan sends it through the seat foam. The circuits labeled heater in this connector therefore belong to an air-temperature control function that can heat or cool, rather than proving the seat only has resistance-heating elements.

sections.title: The junction passes several kinds of circuits
sections.body: The assignments distinguish cushion and backrest thermal-device pairs, fan paths, blower-speed control and temperature-sensing paths. An inline connection simply carries these circuits between harness sections. A disrupted path can affect power, a command or feedback, so a seat-comfort concern does not automatically identify a failed blower assembly.

sections.title: The two face descriptions differ
sections.body: Some male-face entries use passenger-indicator or driver-heater-switch labels where the female face names driver-backrest temperature and blower control. Wire-size alternatives also appear. Preserve those face-specific descriptions and resolve them through the wiring reference rather than treating the male and female text as identical. The housing and unused positions do not establish additional functions.

topics.title: Seat Climate Harness Junction with Network Paths
topics.summary: C3808 joins harnesses 14D230 and 14A005. Its tables include driver-seat climate-control paths and medium-speed network connections, combining operating circuits and communication in one inline housing.

sections.title: Temperature conditioning and airflow work together
sections.body: The front seat climate system uses a Thermo-Electric Device (TED), fan and temperature sensor in each cushion and backrest blower assembly. The TED heats or cools cabin air, and the blower distributes it through the seat foam. Heater labels in the connector table refer to these conditioning paths and do not describe the whole system’s cooling capability.

sections.title: Separate network traffic from operating power
sections.body: The table includes cushion and backrest thermal-device pairs, fan paths, temperature feedback, blower-speed control and a Medium-Speed Controller Area Network (MS-CAN) high/low pair. Network wires carry messages; they do not supply blower-motor power. C3808 is the separable connection carrying those paths, not the controller that interprets messages or regulates the seat.

sections.title: Compare the mating faces without inventing agreement
sections.body: The male table contains passenger-indicator and driver-heater-switch labels where the female table identifies driver-backrest temperature and speed-control paths. Those differences, along with wire-detail differences, must remain visible. Match the listed circuit and harness identities to the applicable schematic instead of inferring that every label describes the same function on both halves.

connector-C226A.summary: The steering column mechanically connects the steering wheel to the steering gear; C226A belongs to the nearby steering column control module, which interfaces with the wheel and column switches. This 12-cavity view maps its supply, ground, communication and feature-specific circuits, including the applicable SelectShift paddle connections.

G1726383.summary: See how the steering column, upper shaft, lower shaft and coupling form the mechanical connection from the steering wheel to the steering gear. The lower shaft is collapsible, and the source requires a measurement whenever it is disconnected from the upper shaft or coupling.

G1693270.summary: This procedure removes and refits the SCCM assembly and its electrical connections. If a new module is being installed, its scan-tool configuration process begins with the old SCCM still connected and is completed after the replacement is fitted.

G1702174.summary: This procedure replaces the electronic column lock, including access, its special retaining fasteners and the configuration work required for a new module. The BCM configuration and training steps are part of making the replacement lock operate correctly.

connector-C2434.summary: C2434 is the steering column lock module’s four-cavity connector. Its view identifies an unused position and separate supply, ground and LIN circuits, helping you distinguish the lock wiring from the SCCM connector beside the steering wheel.

G1693265.summary: This overview connects the steering-column stalks, steering-wheel buttons and applicable paddle switches with the functions they control. It also introduces the push-button ignition and column-lock systems, whose modules and connectors have different roles.

G1693266.summary: This reference explains how push-button ignition and the electronic column lock interact with the BCM, vehicle networks and start authorization. Use its system diagrams and operating conditions to understand the lock’s power, communication and configuration requirements.

wiring-081-003.summary: This diagram traces the SCCM’s LIN and separate high-speed-wiper circuits to the windshield-wiper motor, then shows the motor’s related washer and ground connections. Its rain-sensitive branch is identified separately, so follow the equipment-specific path.

wiring-030-003.summary: This 6R80 diagram follows the upshift, downshift and signal-return circuits through the SCCM connection and clockspring to the steering-wheel paddle switches. It describes the automatic-transmission paddle arrangement rather than every Mustang steering wheel.

wiring-112-003.summary: This Security Pack wiring diagram shows the column lock’s supply relay, BCM control and monitoring, LIN communication and ground path. Match it to the vehicle’s equipment before using its connector and circuit references.
